Comment: First comes the announcement.  "Nothing will change." "The studio will remain independent." "Our vision stays exactly the same."  I've heard this speech so many times from so many companies that I've honestly lost count.  When Sandbox Interactive was acquired by Stillfront in 2020, players were told exactly that. The game design philosophy wouldn't change. The roadmap wouldn't change. The team would remain in control.  Maybe that was true at the time.  But look at Albion today and ask yourself one question:  Does this still feel like a game designed around what players enjoy, or around engagement metrics and revenue?  Take the proposed dynamic spawn rates. Who benefits from making off-peak gameplay less rewarding?  Certainly not the player who works night shifts. Not the parent who only gets to play after midnight. Not people living outside the server's primary timezone.  The only thing it really accomplishes is funneling everyone into peak hours, where activity numbers look better and players compete harder for everything.  Then look at the continued erosion of solo content.  Every few updates, another activity gets less rewarding.' Another incentive to play the way SBI wants instead of the way you want. Another reason to log in during prime time. Another reason to join bigger groups. Another reason to stay engaged on their terms instead of yours.  Maybe every single one of these changes can be justified individually. But together? They paint a pattern. And that's exactly what worries me. Because this is what happens to so many successful games after they're acquired. The conversation slowly shifts away from "Is this fun?"  Towards:  "Does this improve engagement?" "Does this improve retention?" "Does this improve revenue?"  Those aren't the same question.  The saddest part is that Albion didn't become successful because it chased KPIs.  It became successful because it trusted its players.  One global world. Player freedom. Play how you want. Progress however you want.  Now we've got server splits with no meaningful transfer path, increasingly restrictive progression changes, solo content getting chipped away, and mechanics that make playing outside prime time feel worse instead of better. I'm not saying investors are personally designing Albion. I'm saying public companies have one job: increase shareholder value.  When a studio becomes part of that machine, the pressure changes. Sometimes you don't ruin a game by adding pay-to-win. Sometimes you ruin it by making hundreds of small decisions that each look reasonable on paper—but all push in the same direction.  Players don't quit because of one bad patch. They quit because, after years of "small optimizations," they wake up one day and realize they're no longer playing the game they fell in love with.  That's what I'm afraid is happening to Albion.

Video: Albion Online | Dragonfire Update Introduction
Comment: One of the things I miss the most in Albion is a truly engaging PvE experience. Right now, most PvE encounters feel very repetitive. Bosses usually have a couple of simple skill shots, an enormous health pool, and that's about it.  The difficulty doesn't come from mastering mechanics—it comes from spending several minutes hitting a target with hundreds of thousands of HP. Bosses rarely have meaningful mechanics, different combat phases, evolving move sets, or attacks that require players to adapt their strategy.  I believe Albion would greatly benefit from a more challenging, skill-based PvE system. Players should have to dodge abilities, learn mechanics, react to different phases, and develop strategies instead of simply dealing damage until the boss dies.  This kind of content wouldn't only improve PvE—it would also attract PvP players like myself, who eventually left the game because the gameplay became too repetitive. A PvE experience that rewards mechanical skill and decision-making would make Albion far more engaging for every type of player.  There is one point mentioned in the video that I completely disagree with.  I don't think open-world bosses should have very long spawn timers that allow guilds to prepare far in advance. If a powerful boss is announced 24 hours before it appears, the outcome becomes predictable.  This is exactly what already happens with the 8.4 resource nodes. The strongest guilds always secure them because they have plenty of time to organize dozens of players. Smaller or mid-sized guilds simply cannot compete against a top-tier alliance that has an entire day to prepare.  I believe the same thing will happen with the dragons unless this system is carefully balanced.  Instead, the game should lean more toward immediate or short-notice events. For example, if a dragon is going to spawn in one hour—or even with less notice—it creates opportunities for many different guilds to participate. It rewards awareness, quick reactions, and active gameplay rather than just organizational power.  Otherwise, the biggest PvP guilds will permanently control this content and prevent newer or developing guilds from accessing important resources and experiencing the new PvE content.

Comment: Honestly, patch notes and update news always reach everyone one way or another, and that takes away some of the fun. I want to make it clear that I am not just speaking for myself, but for a large part of the community that has its own playstyle: players who want to truly immerse themselves and dive deep into the world of Albion, eager to soak up everything it has to offer beyond just trading and the usual routine. If a dragon suddenly flew past me without me having the slightest clue it even existed in the game, it would be so much more exciting! It would feel like a new player discovering mechanics and locations from updates released long ago. That is what real hype feels like. It makes sense to announce minor visual tweaks or quality-of-life adjustments, but something as massive and breathtaking as a dragon appearing in the lands of Albion is not something you see every day, and not everyone should know about it right off the bat. Even if the news eventually reached us word-of-mouth instead of through an official announcement, it would still be thrilling, as it would create a temporary legend, a true myth waiting to be uncovered. It would have been incredible content for the creators who love this game so much. Anyway, it is just the opinion of an old veteran who, despite a little complaining, genuinely loved the Dragon's Fire update and cannot wait for the release!

Comment: You've changed the direction of the game by reducing the original PvE experience and putting more emphasis on PvP. How is that supposed to keep this game alive?  The new dragon content has the same problem. Players are expected to risk expensive, high-tier gear for rewards that simply aren't worth it. Even if the total market value is technically the same, it is mostly made up of low-value loot that nobody actually wants.  I play both PvE and PvP, so I am not against PvP itself. The problem is that, over the past two years, PvE has become noticeably worse with almost every update. Players who enjoy running dungeons, Gold Chests, or other PvE content—and those who simply are not interested in PvP—have been left with fewer and fewer meaningful activities.  PvE is one of the core pillars of Albion Online. Not every player wants to participate in PvP, and not everyone has the experience, time, or ability to compete in PvP content. How are these players supposed to continue enjoying the game if their preferred playstyle keeps being neglected?  PvE players are also an important part of the game's economy. They gather resources, craft items, generate loot, and help maintain the market. Without a healthy PvE population, the entire economy and player ecosystem will eventually suffer.  I am not asking for PvP to be removed or ignored. I enjoy both sides of the game. But please stop changing or damaging well-designed content and enjoyable gameplay just to force more players into PvP. Albion Online should allow PvE and PvP to grow together, instead of sacrificing one side to benefit the other.  The Asian server has another major issue: it is overwhelmingly dominated by Chinese players. You say you want to create a healthy PvP environment, but I honestly do not see it.  What we actually experience during large-scale battles is constant server lag caused by the widespread use of network accelerators. Meanwhile, the players using them seem barely affected, while everyone else has to deal with the lag.  So I want to ask: **Are you actually planning to address these issues, or are you choosing to ignore them because Chinese players spend more money? If so, is it worth losing more and more players from other regions?  I hope the developers can understand that Albion Online's strength comes from the balance between different types of players. Comment: The new content is great, but I hope you reconsider the recent changes to both Open World and Static Dungeon boss spawn timers.  While the mob buffs are welcome, the increased boss respawn timers make clearing these objectives feel far less rewarding. Bosses and their chests are the primary source of value, and spending more time waiting than actually fighting hurts the overall gameplay loop.  These changes also reduce organic PvP. Static Dungeons have always been natural hotspots where static players and normal fame farm groups contest objectives and create spontaneous fights. With fewer boss spawns, there's simply less reason for players to stay or contest these areas aside from pure fame farming.  I'm also not sure what data these changes were based on. During peak hours, most Black Zone players are participating in ZvZs or roaming for PvP rather than doing this content. Slowing down boss spawns only makes these activities feel less engaging and less worth contesting, especially during dynamic events (rally). The same goes for Ava roads. Not everyone has a whole day waiting for a proper and worthy Ava camp to clear, with spawn timers ranging from 40 mins to 3 hours.   Please consider reverting the spawn timer changes. They reduce both the rewards and the player interactions that make these activities fun.

Comment: Question, what do you mean by progress in Albion online. I am currently struggling to find out what progress means in Albion online. For example in WoW. Progress means defeating Raid Bosses in Raid finder difficulty, get that gear, move on to the next difficulty tear get that gear till you fully acquired mythic gear BiS items. This is the path of PvE. Then there is PvP where you grind through ranked BG's and Arenas to climb through ladder.  So far what I got with Albion is, get in to BZ, farm silver/fame, get back, get in to BZ again farm more silver/fame, get back, wanna PvP solo in BZ and hunt people down? No can't do with Kingmaker, have to change your loadout to something viable since anybody you try to solo gank just mounts up and leaves. So that is actually locked behind other gear setups. Not that it means any kind of progress. You just happen to earn more money if you manage to kill someone. It doesn't get you anything in particular or a sense of accomplishment. So is Albion all about earning silver? Is there something that actually progress ingame? Ofc I'm not talking about progress charts in the activities window. So far the one thing I think that gives you decent progress feeling is Faction Warfare and Infamy thing(which is broken imo in corrupted dungeons. It expects you to win every single PvP fight in a rock, paper, scissors equipment environment).  To me the primary cons of Albion is:  1. The lack of "feeling" of progression throughout the majority of the content. BZ feels like it revolves around groups of 5-15 players going medieval on solo players butts while from solo players perspective PvP means surviving and managing to get back to home with your loot. So all progress comes down to making silver and making more of it more efficiently. You don't gain actual in-game fame other than your name in the ladder-board, which is kind of boring tbh. After all its just a spreadsheet with a bunch of names and numbers no in-game prescence or difference provided to the no1 guy which I believe the core of lack of progress. A title that gives actual in-game edge (Like "King of Fort Sterling". Earns percentage of sales taxes, bigass statue of the player built inside the city etc.)  2. "If you wanna do this activity, you have to use this equipment otherwise you are going to lose" style design and balancing. Like why the hell am I forced to put on an assasin's west in order to "force" people to fight me in open world. Or why do I always have to play the "prey" role for 15 gankers with my Kingmaker loadout in openworld which I can only do PvE and everybody I try to actually hunt or fight runs from me. Question is why do I have to wear something viable in order to be able to choose my fights. I think this kills the freedom in a sandbox game where it is advertised as "Wear whatever you want". "Play however you like.". Well I want to be able to play Kingmaker with soldiers armor and royal helmet combo, farming in BZ while being able to do PvP but PvP part is just me running from gankers and not being able to get someone fight me 1v1. So I am forced to use a claymore with assasins west or some other gear that is actually viable. So the game deosn't truly give you "freedom" afterall. I think if you build a system like this you HAVE to make everything balanced and viable. I believe game needs tweaks in its core mechanics like mounting etc.  3. Lack of grading in BZ. I think having BZ not graded leads to bad playing experience. I think zones should be gated with ip/fame where more lucrative zones available to players with more ip and less lucrative zones should only be available to low ip. Result? Balanced fights, new players either fight with smurfs or fellow new players. Sense of actual progress.  Albion is a great game it just need a few refinements in its core mechanics and overall design. It's like this great dish that lacks the perfect sauce on top. It's absolutely delicious but it is missing some stuff.

Comment: @raedabed3834 It has really good crafting, grinding and progression ontop of a lot of diversity.  And in my opinion the absolute best PvP there is - in no other game can you trash a group of 50 players with just 6-10 people through sheer skill, experience, timing and knowledge. It has a deep strategic element to it as well, on small, mid and large PvP scale.  It also has a great community, people who can actually deal with loss and are battle hardened, like really based people who dont give a shit about your feelings, that game is a warzone. People who have a soul, whom you can have some real talk with and most of the guys i got to know while being in of the top guilds were all unique, they were people who had their own minds and own opinions and werent scared to speak such. Unlike most other MMORPGs where its all about the wheather and being nice on the surface level. One word of critsism and they break down, i couldnt stand that playing WoW-TBC just recently. No room for mental pussies, frankly.  People die, lose hours of work, get up, regear and move right back into battle since some of these fights can go on many minutes to even hours, depending on the scale and the objective and how many different parties are involved. Not uncommon for 3-4 different guilds fighting each other, so you basically get pulp fiction scenarios.  Adrenaline rushes? First time i ever experienced it playing a game was Albion Online. My heart rate went 200 first time i got chased in the Black Zone with decent gear/loot.  The problem though: -It has instanced zones, so it lacks the open world feeling -Its PvE can be challenging, but is always tied to some PvP. Everything that has meaning in this game is PvP. You can do meaningful progression without PvP, but once you tasted blood and hauled thick loot through PvP or PvP tied PvE, it stops feeling rewarding.  Hence i said half the game we all want.  Last but not least: it has a VERY STEEP learning curve.  The game really opens up once you grinded your way into a top guild, they always looking for new blood that has a gamer sense. So you can assume to first put in 100h of grind/exploration to get the basics down and then another 500-1000hours to get the necessary experience. You only learn through dying, which is the hardest part.
